names.name: Qur'an pendant
names.said: Āyat al-Kursī, the Throne Verse — the text most often inside one

text.what: A metal case at the throat with scripture inside it. Sometimes a whole miniature Qur'an, protected by an illuminated metal cover; sometimes a single verse on paper or engraved on the metal itself. The verse is most often Āyat al-Kursī, the Throne Verse, Qur'an 2:255 — the 255th verse of the second chapter, and the one the tradition names the greatest in the book. Others hang the same verse framed on a wall or from a mirror in a car.
text.story:
The verse opens: "Allah: there is no god but Him, the Ever-Living, the Ever-Watchful. Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him." It is built concentrically, in the symmetry most common in the Qur'an, where each segment answers its pair across a centre.

What the tradition says it does is on the record in hadith and in commentary, and this atlas reports it without weighing it. Reciting the verse is said in hadith to ward off devils, šayāṭīn, and fiends, ʿafārīt; recited after every obligatory prayer it is held to admit the reciter to Paradise with nothing in the way but death. Al-Suyuti narrates a man of humanity meeting a man of the jinn, and the jinn, beaten in a wrestling match, teaching him the verse that keeps any devil from entering his house with him — this one. The Throne Verse is used in exorcism, against jinn and devils. Because it is associated with protection, the tradition also reads it as a shield against the evil eye. It is recited before a journey and before sleep, morning and evening as a daily adhkār.

The material tradition round it is documented. Miniature Qur'ans kept in illuminated metal cases are one form; block-printed text amulets sealed into lead cases with lugs, so they could be sewn on or hung, are another. Preferred materials are precious and semi-precious, and the reasons given for them are explicit: carnelian, ʿaqīq, is favoured because it was counted the stone of Muhammad, who was said to have worn a carnelian seal set in silver on the little finger of his right hand; jade and jasper are held to assure victory in battle, guard against lightning and treat diseases of the internal organs. A combination of jade and carnelian is read for fertility and embryogenesis — the reddish, light-carrying carnelian standing for blood, which echoes the clot of congealed blood God created the human from, Qur'an 96:2.

*Inference —* the cited accounts are careful to separate early Islamic amulets from what came before them: these appeal to God in the first instance, where Byzantine, Roman and early Iranian magic addressed demonic forces or the spirits of the dead. That is a claim about direction of address, not about efficacy, and it is the line the tradition's own scholars keep returning to when they argue about whether to wear one at all.

dating.note: No dated earliest Qur'an pendant was read. The floor here is the dated class of medieval Islamic text amulets in metal cases the Amulet article describes, from the tenth or eleventh century. The verse itself is seventh-century. Treat the floor as the object's, not the practice's.

object.made_by: handwritten by a scribe for those who could pay; serialised block-printed copies in sealed lead cases for those who could not
object.inscription: Āyat al-Kursī, Qur'an 2:255, or a miniature complete Qur'an; on printed cases, surat al-Ikhlas stamped into the lead
object.note: No published measurement was read for a pendant; the related printed packet in the Aga Khan Museum is 7.2 × 5.5 cm and is recorded on the ta'wiz record.
